quickAnswer: Indian traditions offer frameworks rather than a single rulebook. Many speak of the four aims of life (dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation) balanced within right conduct; the Gita urges acting from one's own duty without selfish attachment; Jainism centres non-harm; Buddhism the Eightfold Path; Sikh thought honest work, sharing and remembrance of God; and the Tirukkural a practical ethics of virtue, wealth and love. They differ in emphasis, but most tie a good life to inner discipline and care for others.

perspectives.view: The Gita, central to Vedantic ethics, asks one to act according to one's own duty as an offering, with equanimity and without selfish attachment.
Jainism centres life on non-harm (ahimsa), truthfulness and non-possessiveness, with vows scaled for lay people and ascetics.
The Buddhist path combines ethical conduct, meditation and wisdom, with friendliness and compassion toward all beings.
Sikh teaching summarises the good life as honest work, sharing with others and remembrance of the Name, lived as a householder rather than in withdrawal.
The Tirukkural addresses virtue, wealth and love in practical terms, from friendship and hospitality to governance.
The epics teach largely through character and story: the Ramayana holds up ideals of conduct, while the Mahabharata dwells on hard moral choices.
